earlier_scan.note: Title indicates tonal prosody (downstep) rather than stress; PDF unreachable so no statement read.

new_statements.quote: Pukur has three primitive units making use of pitch variation, a H(igh tone), a unit analyzed as a downstep /Ť/, and a post-downstepped high tone (HŤ), which contrast with each other as well as with the absence of any unit (Ø). No form of stress (as defined by LEHISTE (1970: 106–120) as “linguistically significant prosody” manifested in the acoustic signal due to “differences in physical effort” and “degree of force,” with such phonetic correlates as intensity, fundamental frequency and duration) was detected, whether it be phonemic, morphological, or bound (as per LEHISTE’s (1970) terminology).
new_statements.citation: Rochant, Neige. 2023. A Bilectal Grammar of Baga Pukur: An Atlantic Language of Guinea. PhD thesis, Université Sorbonne Nouvelle - Paris 3 (NNT 2023PA030111), HAL tel-05618821. Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.1 Phoneme inventory, p. 50.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, §2.1 Phoneme inventory, p. 50 (PDF page 81); supporting passages §2.5.3.2 p. 181, §2.5.6 p. 227, §2.5.7 pp. 229-231
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (pdfinfo: 1033 pages, title 'A Bilectal Grammar of Baga Pukur: an Atlantic Language of Guinea', author Neige Rochant) and re-extracted PDF page 81 with extracted text: it is printed page 50, running head 'Chapter 2 Phonology', end of §2.1 just before '2.2 Consonants'. The quoted passage is there word for word: 'Pukur has three primitive units making use of pitch variation, a H(igh tone), a unit analyzed as a downstep /Ť/, and a post-downstepped high tone (HŤ), which contrast with each other as well as with the absence of any unit (Ø). No form of stress (as defined by LEHISTE (1970: 106–120) as "linguistically significant prosody"...) was detected, whether it be phonemic, morphologica…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Pukur is a tone language (high tone, an underlying downstep, and a post-downstepped high, all contrasting with the absence of a toneme); the grammar explicitly reports that no stress of any kind - phonemic, morphological or bound - was detected. The author notes that native nouns carry at most one /H/ (culminativity), which could invite a 'pitch accent' label she rejects synchronically, and hypothesises a former word-accent system as the diachronic source of the tone system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable; no stress reported at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the no-stress statement. Related remarks: H-tone spreading stops at the penultimate TBU, which the author says 'suggests a principle of penultimate prominence' (§2.5.3.2, p. 181); French loanwords with final stress are borrowed with the falling /HŤ/ toneme on the final syllable (§2.5.3.5, ~p. 208); the plural suffix and attributive suffix carry an underlying downstep possibly reflecting a former recessive accented clitic (§2.5.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; the tonal domain is the prosodic word in nouns and the morpheme in verbs (§2.5.6, p. 227). The no-stress statement applies to the language as a whole, both dialects (M'Bottiny = PuMb and Binari = PuBn), based on 8.5 months of fieldwork 2019-2023 and a 6.5-hour text corpus.
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar's 'Pukur' / 'Baga Pukur' is the language known in older sources (via Soso) as Baga Mboteni and Baga Binari; Rochant treats these as the two dialects (PuMb, M'Bottiny; PuBn, Binari) of one language (thesis pp. 5-6), which matches Glottolog baga1275 / ISO bcg exactly. The stress statement covers both dialects.

sources.citation: Rochant, Neige. 2023. Tonemeless syllables in Pukur. Handout, Theory of Tone Workshop, LLACAN/INaLCO, Paris, 30 Nov 2023 (HAL hal-05629163), 8 pp.
sources.note: Purely tonal description (TBU = syllable; tonemes /H/, /Ť/, /HŤ/ vs Ø; H spreads rightward and stops at the penultimate TBU, 'penultimate prominence / non-finality constraint'). No mention of stress.
